## Hauora Māori — Health Outcomes for Māori in Aotearoa

The health gap between Māori and non-Māori in New Zealand is one of the country's most persistent and well-documented inequities. While there have been meaningful improvements over time, Māori continue to experience poorer health outcomes across almost every measure compared to non-Māori.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## Life Expectancy

The most striking headline statistic is the gap in life expectancy. According to the most recent Stats NZ data (2022–2024), Māori life expectancy at birth is 75.8 years — the lowest of any ethnic group in New Zealand [[1]](cite://1/1). By comparison, people who identify as Pākehā or other ethnicities have a life expectancy of 82.8 years, a gap of roughly seven years [[1]](cite://1/2)[[2]](cite://2/1).

There is a positive note here, however: Māori life expectancy has increased by 3.1 years from the 2005–2007 period to 2022–2024, a larger increase than any other ethnic group over the same timeframe [[1]](cite://1/3). Earlier data from 2012–2014 recorded life expectancy at birth as 77 years for Māori women and 73 years for Māori men, compared to 84 years for non-Māori women and 80 years for non-Māori men [[3]](cite://3/1)[[4]](cite://4/1).

On average, Māori die younger than non-Māori — a pattern consistently recorded in national data [[5]](cite://5/1).

## Chronic Disease

The disparities extend across a wide range of serious conditions:

**Heart disease** is one of the starkest examples. A 2025 report by Otago University, commissioned by the Kia Manawanui Trust, found that Māori and Pasifika (Pacific peoples) die from heart disease on average ten years younger than Pākehā [[6]](cite://6/1)[[7]](cite://7/1). Māori also have the highest rate of death from heart disease of any ethnic group in New Zealand [[8]](cite://8/1). Data from the 2010s showed Māori were dying from heart disease at more than twice the rate of non-Māori [[9]](cite://9/1).

**Cancer** figures are similarly concerning. In the 2010s, Māori men were almost three times as likely as non-Māori men to die of lung cancer; Māori women were over four times as likely as non-Māori women [[9]](cite://9/2).

**Diabetes** has reached near-epidemic levels in some Māori communities. Māori were twice as likely as non-Māori to have diabetes, with higher complication rates as well [[9]](cite://9/3). In the 2000s, it was estimated that well over half of those with diabetes in some Māori communities didn't even know they had it [[10]](cite://10/1).

## Child and Youth Health

Māori and Pasifika children are disproportionately affected by respiratory conditions, rheumatic fever and heart disease, skin infections, dental disease, and mental health problems [[11]](cite://11/1). Hospitalisation rates for respiratory conditions among Māori and Pasifika children have been largely attributed to disparities in access to warm, dry housing — a direct consequence of income inequality [[12]](cite://12/1).

While there have been some improvements — meningococcal admissions and skin infection rates among young Māori declined between 2010 and 2014 — the rates of skin infections among Māori aged 0–24 remained twice as high as those for non-Māori youth even after that decline [[12]](cite://12/2).

## Mental Health

The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission's latest reporting (June 2026) paints a troubling picture. Some 22.5 percent of Māori experienced "high" or "very high" psychological distress in the four weeks prior to being surveyed — well above the 14 percent national average [[13]](cite://13/1). The age-standardised rate of suicide deaths is highest among Māori men aged 25 to 44 years [[14]](cite://14/1)[[15]](cite://15/1).

Despite this elevated need, Māori are not being adequately prioritised for mental health support. Fewer people can access kaupapa Māori (Māori-centred) primary mental health services, funding for those services has not kept pace with broader mental health investment, and only 29 percent of Māori accessing specialist services use kaupapa Māori services [[14]](cite://14/2)[[15]](cite://15/2).

In inpatient settings, Māori in adult services were 6.6 times more likely to be placed in seclusion (solitary confinement) than non-Māori — a practice the commission describes as often traumatising [[15]](cite://15/3).

## Access to Care

Access to healthcare remains a significant barrier. Factors including cost, availability of doctors, geographic isolation, and the attitudes of medical personnel all contribute to poorer health outcomes for Māori [[10]](cite://10/2). Māori living in rural areas face compounding disadvantages — Māori under 30 living remotely were twice as likely to die from a preventable disease as their urban peers [[16]](cite://16/1).

Research also shows that Māori with mental health conditions were 7.7 percent more likely than non-Māori to report difficulties securing a GP appointment, with experiences of feeling less heard and respected by healthcare providers [[17]](cite://17/1).

## A Long-Standing Inequity

These disparities are not new. Health differences between Māori and Pākehā have been documented since the 19th century, and despite significant improvements — particularly in the decades following World War II — the gap has proven stubbornly persistent [[18]](cite://18/1)[[19]](cite://19/1). As researchers note, despite great improvements and a significant rise in life expectancy, Māori are still worse affected than non-Māori by almost every known health condition [[9]](cite://9/4).

The causes are understood to be deeply structural — rooted in poverty, housing quality, access to healthcare, and the legacy of historical inequities [[10]](cite://10/3)[[11]](cite://11/2).

Would you like to explore what specific policies or initiatives have been introduced to address these health disparities for Māori?

2.document_title: Te Hauora Māori: A Comprehensive History of Māori Health in New Zealand from Pre-European Times to the 20th Century
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori health across multiple centuries, from pre-European times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Before European contact, Māori were generally fit and healthy with life expectancy around 28-30 years, relying on traditional healing practices involving tohunga (healers), rongoā rākau (plant medicines), and karakia (rituals). European arrival brought devastating diseases like measles, influenza, typhoid, and tuberculosis, causing significant population decline. Land confiscation, poor housing, and unsanitary conditions worsened health outcomes. From 1900 onwards, government health services expanded with the Public Health Department establishing a Māori section led by Dr Māui Pōmare. Despite vaccination campaigns and health education, tuberculosis, typhoid, and the 1918 influenza pandemic devastated Māori communities. The 1938 Social Security Act introduced free hospital admission and universal medical benefits. Post-WWII improvements included successful tuberculosis campaigns and declining infant mortality rates. However, significant health disparities persisted throughout the 20th century, with Māori mortality rates approximately twice that of non-Māori in 1960. Contributing factors included socioeconomic disparities in employment, income, education, and substandard housing. The government gradually adopted a bicultural approach to health, particularly after the 1984 Te Hui Whakaoranga workshop, promoting Māori participation in health planning and recognizing traditional healing practices alongside Western medicine.

5.document_title: Women's Health in New Zealand: Historical Perspectives, Disparities, and Community Activism from Colonial Times to the 21st Century
5.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines women's health in New Zealand from the 1800s to 2000s, analyzing health disparities across ethnic groups. It traces how European colonization introduced infectious diseases that devastated Māori populations while Pākehā women experienced improved health. Key findings reveal significant inequities: non-Māori women born in 2007 could expect to live 83 years versus 75.1 for Māori women. Maternal mortality for Māori women reached 23 per 1,000 live births in 1920, compared to 6.5 for Pākehā women. By the 2000s, major causes of death were cancer, cardiovascular disease, and respiratory disease, with Māori women experiencing cardiovascular disease at 4.2 times higher rates and diabetes mortality 10 times higher. Pacific Island women faced elevated mortality from heart disease, stroke, and diabetes, with 48% obesity rates. The document extensively covers health activism including the Young Māori Party (1889), Women's Christian Temperance Union, Te Puea Hērangi's medical clinics, the Family Planning Association (1936), the Māori Women's Welfare League (1951), and feminist health activism of the 1970s-1980s including the cervical cancer scandal. It highlights Māori-centered health models incorporating emotional, physical, whānau, and spiritual wellbeing that challenged mainstream healthcare approaches.

35.document_title: Māori Students in Medical Admissions Scheme Show Higher Graduation Rates
35.document_summary: Research published in The New Zealand Medical Journal demonstrates that Māori and Pacific students participating in the Māori and Pacific Admissions Scheme (MAPAS) at the University of Auckland graduate at significantly higher rates than other Māori and Pacific students. Established in 1972, MAPAS provides comprehensive support including a foundation programme (Hikitia te Ora), academic assistance, pastoral care, and cultural support throughout students' degrees. Dr Rhys Jones reports that MAPAS students achieve pass and graduation rates 15-23 percentage points higher than average. The programme addresses critical health workforce inequities, as only 5.1% of medical practitioners are Māori and 2.4% are Pacific people—far below population representation. Pro-equity programmes like MAPAS are essential for producing a culturally competent health workforce that can better serve underserved communities and address persistent health inequities in Aotearoa New Zealand.

[Page 1] Cure Kids says a new study shows Pasifika children in Aotearoa are 115 times more likely to be hospitalised with acute rheumatic fever than European children. The fourth State of Child Health Report showed Pasifika, Māori and children in low socio economic areas were disproportionately affected by respiratory conditions, rheumatic fever and heart disease, skin infections, dental disease and mental health problems. Cure Kids head Frances Soutter said urgent national action was needed to ensure all tamariki and rangatahi had access to proper healthcare, housing and nutrition to reverse the trend. "Too many of our children are experiencing preventable illnesses, with the burden falling disproportionately on Māori, Pasifika, and those living in areas of high deprivation. By targeting these risk factors, we can reverse these trends and generate long term benefits for New Zealand's population that far exceed the initial costs," Soutter said. The report developed in collaboration with the NZ Child and Youth Epidemiology Service at the University of Otago showed a 44 percent increase in the number of children under a year old being hospitalised with respiratory problems over the last 20 years. It said respiratory conditions were the leading cause of acute hospitalisations for children, with infants under one year being particularly vulnerable. The University of Auckland's Dr Anneka Anderson said the study was a "huge wake up call" that more needed to be done to address poverty and poor living conditions and break down barriers to healthcare. She said a one size fits all approach to health would only make matters worse. "Saying that we should treat everyone the same actually promotes inequity. It's a bit like saying we shouldn't have special carparks for non able bodied people. "We have different services to try and level up the playing field, and taking that away always leads to a disaster." She said the Covid 19 pandemic had provided an ideal case study to show the power of tailoring a health response towards ethnic and cultural groups. "The government responded with a one size fits all approach and we saw huge differences in vaccine uptake for Māori than for non Māori. As soon as the control and resources were handed back to Māori providers to provide a 'for Māori, by Māori' service we saw the uptake increase. "So we see that this rhetoric that ethnicity doesn't count and shouldn't be taken into account for different health services hasn't worked in the past, and there's no way it's going to work in the future." Anderson said in addition to working to address poverty and basic living wages health services needed to be designed with a "rights based lens" to cut the inequities across the population. "We live in such a resource rich country. [Typically] in low economic countries we see these high rates of rheumatic heart disease. In Aotearoa we shouldn't be seeing those. "When we compared different groups of Pacific adults, the rates of diagnosed mood and anxiety disorders were higher among those born in Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ born) than overseas born Pacific, with rates appearing to increase as time spent in Aotearoa New Zealand increased," she said. The research team examined five consecutive years of data from the annual New Zealand Health Survey (NZHS), spanning 2014/15 2018/19. "In this circumstance, a lot of Pacific researchers talk about the impact of acculturation, which is how our culture changes as Pacific people when we've migrated from our Pacific ancestral homeland to Aotearoa, New Zealand. "The things that come along with that ...when population groups migrate to another country is the weakening or the loss of our social structures and also it disrupts the way we transmit our cultures. "And we have to take on a new language, and so our language declines as well." Ataera Minster referred to a phenomonen known as the "healthy immigrant effect". "So we come and our health outcomes are slightly better than people that are already living here. And then over time, you see this decline, and again to do with the stresses associated with that acculturation process. 46.document_summary: A new Otago University report commissioned by cardiac advocacy charity Kia Manawanui Trust reveals critical failures in New Zealand's cardiac care system. Key findings show that half of all heart attack patients are not treated within internationally accepted timeframes, and New Zealand has only one-third of the cardiologists it needs. The report calculates the total cost of heart disease to the economy at $13.8 billion annually. Significant disparities exist, with Māori and Pacific people hospitalized or dying from heart disease over a decade earlier than other New Zealanders. Regional variations are stark, with areas having the highest death rates (Tairāwhiti, Lakes, Whanganui, Taranaki) having the fewest cardiac specialists. The workforce shortage is severe, with cardiology sonographers declining from 70.4 in 2013 to 43.5 in 2024 despite population growth. The trust calls for immediate government investment in cardiac infrastructure and a national strategy to recruit and retain cardiology staff.

[Page 1] Mental health patients find it harder to access GPs, study finds ByRayssa Almeida Reporter 2024 11 29 06:28:35+13:00 Mental health patients in New Zealand face significantly worse experiences in primary healthcare compared to those without mental health conditions, according to a national study conducted by the University of Otago. The study, published in the New Zealand Medical Journal, analysed responses from a Health Quality and Safety Commission survey that asked about people's experiences with general practice services. The findings revealed critical barriers to accessing care, with 26.8 percent of mental health patients unable to secure a GP appointment in the past year, compared to 19.6 percent of the general population. Deep rooted systemic issues Ruth Cunningham Lead researcher Ruth Cunningham said the disparities reflected deep rooted systemic issues, including stigma and the pressures on the healthcare system itself. "When the system is under stress... our cognitive biases come through, and we're even more likely to treat people differently because of those biases," she said. "In those cases... providers [need to] think about the experience that people with mental health conditions are having [at the doctor.. but [it] can become harder when the system is under stress." Cunningham emphasised the importance of medical professionals being aware of their biases and how these affect patient care. "The way in which a diagnosis of mental health conditions, problematic substance or addiction, can get in the way of providing high quality care is not something that is often talked about, but is a very important issue." Stigma also discourages patients from seeking care, Cunningham noted. "Experiences of stigma and discrimination... understandably [lead people to] disconnect from the provider or they simply don't go back." Connection and representation The study highlighted that disparities were even more significant for Māori with mental health conditions, who consistently reported greater challenges in accessing care, feeling respected, and having their concerns heard by healthcare providers. For instance, Māori with mental health conditions were 7.7 percent more likely than non Māori to report difficulties in securing a GP appointment within the past year. Cunningham pointed to the need for a more diverse healthcare workforce to improve patient provider relationships. "For Māori, the difference in care was exacerbated... even more adverse experiences of care," she said. "This is all about connection and relationships... and increasing Māori and Pasifika healthcare workforce representation. The patient needs to connect to their providers and, if that doesn't happen, they might not come back to seek treatment." Despite the disparities, Cunningham said there were positive developments within the healthcare system. "But we must continue to listen, address biases, and ensure care meets everyone's needs. Even in a stressed system, treating people with kindness and respect remains essential." Related

She is currently the chief executive of Te Waka Whaiora, a kaupapa Maori mental health and addictions support service based in Porirua. "We talk about choice, you talk about who access's what services, Māori don't have a choice. When you come against 20 non Māori organisations and maybe one Māori organisation within a community they will definitely referred to the non Māori organisation, because either A) there's no trust or B) we're not funded to deliver clinical services," she said. There were a whole range of reasons Māori continued to go to non Māori services and she said it was not that Māori services were not in a position to deliver, they just did not have the funds. "So by the time they do access services they're in a crisis, but there aren't enough services to meet that particular crisis so the burden becomes a whānau burden, and sometimes within all cultures not just Māori whānau are actually the reason why our tangata are where they are." Hine Moeke Murray is chief executive of Te Kupenga Net Trust, based in Gisborne, a kaupapa Maori organisation providing peer support and advocacy in mental health and addictions. She said a huge part of the issue was that many Māori did not meet the criteria for intervention. "It's no longer intervention, it's no longer prevention we are doing critical response to our whānau because they couldn't get through the doors in the first place." Without stable funding and strong relationships with clinical services it's very difficult to achieve better outcomes for whānau Māori, she said. "When we talk about intervention our whānau can come to a community organisation absolutely, if they need further clinical intervention because they may need some specialist care and they don't meet the criteria of that service where to from there? Where to from there? They get bounced back into the community and when something goes wrong it's the community organisation that's blamed." Services were jumping through hoops to meet the political outcomes the government of the day required, which created huge pressures on services as well, she said. "If there's no services out there that can meet the needs of our babies, all of our people, then how do we change the system because it is system driven." Koha said there were pockets of funding going out to Māori services, but not enough to make positive long term outcomes. The system was still not meeting the needs of rangatahi, she said. "We have a rangatahi portion within our contract but we don't have a clinical [portion], so what I've had to do is employ clinicians out of some of our little bit of surplus that we have. We're not contracted to do it but we need to do it because I'm finding that that's a gap." "That is why when I launched the Suicide Prevention Action Plan, this had multiple specific actions that were for Māori, to acknowledge those inequities. "I am committed to working with community groups and Health NZ to ensure we are improving outcomes for all New Zealanders, including Māori. That is where the mental health and addiction targets come in. I have been very clear that we are not just celebrating when we reach the targets at a national level. What is most important is getting into the data and ensuring that all groups are reaching the targets. This includes Māori. If there's a region and group not meeting the target, I expect additional focus to be put into that area." "We have invested additional funding, whether it be through the Innovation Fund or the Suicide Prevention Action Plan, for Māori, and I committed to continuing to work with our community organisations to get more funding out the door where needed. The commission's report noted seclusion otherwise known as solitary confinement was often a traumatising experience and the Ministry of Health reported that Māori in adult in patient services were 6.6 times more likely to be secluded than non Māori. Doocey said seclusion was an issue he had been closely looking at and one he cared strongly about addressing, including for Māori. "Each individual case is a clinical decision, and I expect that the appropriate processes and assessments are followed. "The Mental Health Bill currently before Parliament seeks to further reduce the use of seclusion. "The Bill as it currently stands will limit the use of seclusion and strengthen safeguards. It also prohibits the use of seclusion for people under the age of 18. chunkHighlights.text: Life expectancy, mortality and ethnicity

Life expectancy for Māori improved dramatically over the 20th century, and the considerable gap between Māori and Pākehā life expectancy narrowed rapidly after the Second World War. Non-Māori life expectancy

increased rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s, but the increases for Māori were small. However, the gap narrowed in the early 21st century. In 2012-14 life expectancy at birth was 83.9 years for non-Māori women, 80.3 for non-Māori men, 77.1 for Māori women and 73 for Māori men. Life expectancy at birth was 78.7 years for Pasifika females and 74.5 years for Pasifika males.

In the early 21st century Māori had the highest all-age mortality rates, followed by Pacific people. The gap in mortality rates between these two groups and Europeans and others (mainly Asians) widened in the 1980s and 1990s. This was probably related to the economic restructuring of the time, which had a big impact on Māori and Pasifika employment and income. The gap narrowed from the late 1990s to the early 2000s, a time when the economy recovered and health policies began to address health inequalities.
The Asian population (which included a large proportion of recent migrants) had the lowest mortality rate over this period. This reflected the good health of most migrants.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores death and dying practices in New Zealand, covering cultural, religious, and legal dimensions. It traces the evolution of dying locations from home-based care in the 1800s to modern hospital and hospice settings, detailing post-death practices including embalming, Māori tangihanga rituals, funerals, burials, and cremation. The document compares Māori and Pākehā traditions, covering bereavement leave provisions and grief support services. It documents the professionalization of funeral services, with approximately 80 funerals held daily across New Zealand, averaging $8,000-$10,000 in costs. Cremation history is traced from the first society established in Lawrence, Otago in 1875 through modern crematoria, noting the increase in cremation rates from a minority practice in the 1960s to approximately 70% by the 2010s. The document addresses cultural and religious considerations for various faiths and discusses euthanasia, detailing New Zealand's legal journey from prohibition to legalization in 2021 through the End of Life Choice Act. Key statistics indicate that in 2017, 33,339 people died in New Zealand, with median death ages of 78 for men and 83 for women. It emphasizes the importance of rituals and rites across religious and non-religious traditions and the development of hospice care beginning with the Little Company of Mary in 1913.

Age at death still differs significantly for Māori and non-Māori – on average Māori die younger.

9.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori health across multiple centuries, from pre-European times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Before European contact, Māori were generally fit and healthy with life expectancy around 28-30 years, relying on traditional healing practices involving tohunga (healers), rongoā rākau (plant medicines), and karakia (rituals). European arrival brought devastating diseases like measles, influenza, typhoid, and tuberculosis, causing significant population decline. Land confiscation, poor housing, and unsanitary conditions worsened health outcomes. From 1900 onwards, government health services expanded with the Public Health Department establishing a Māori section led by Dr Māui Pōmare. Despite vaccination campaigns and health education, tuberculosis, typhoid, and the 1918 influenza pandemic devastated Māori communities. The 1938 Social Security Act introduced free hospital admission and universal medical benefits. Post-WWII improvements included successful tuberculosis campaigns and declining infant mortality rates. However, significant health disparities persisted throughout the 20th century, with Māori mortality rates approximately twice that of non-Māori in 1960. Contributing factors included socioeconomic disparities in employment, income, education, and substandard housing. The government gradually adopted a bicultural approach to health, particularly after the 1984 Te Hui Whakaoranga workshop, promoting Māori participation in health planning and recognizing traditional healing practices alongside Western medicine.

chunkHighlights.text: Though the gap was closing in the 21st century, clear heath disparities remained. In 2012–14 Māori life expectancy at birth was 6.8 years lower than non-Māori for women and 7.3 years for men. In the 2010s Māori men were almost three times as likely as non-Māori men to die of lung cancer; Māori women were over four times as likely as non-Māori women. Māori died from heart disease at more than twice the rate of non-Māori. Māori were twice as likely to have diabetes as non-Māori, and diabetes complication rates were also higher. Despite great improvements, and a significant rise in life expectancy, Māori were still worse affected than non-Māori by almost every known health condition.

11.fileDescription: A comprehensive State of Child Health Report developed with the NZ Child and Youth Epidemiology Service reveals critical health disparities in Aotearoa New Zealand. The report documents alarming statistics including Pasifika children being 115 times more likely to be hospitalised with acute rheumatic fever compared to European children, and a 44% increase in respiratory hospitalisations for children under one over the past two decades. Pasifika, Māori, and children in low socio-economic areas face disproportionate health burdens from respiratory conditions, rheumatic fever, heart disease, skin infections, dental disease, and mental health problems. Dr Anneka Anderson criticises the government's "one-size-fits-all" health approach, arguing it ignores evidence and perpetuates inequity. The report advocates for tailored, culturally-responsive health services delivered through a "rights-based lens," highlighting the success of COVID-19 vaccine uptake when Māori providers delivered "for Māori, by Māori" services. Cure Kids emphasises that urgent national action is required to address underlying social determinants including poverty, housing, and nutrition to reverse preventable illness trends and achieve equitable health outcomes for all children.

chunkHighlights.text: Cure Kids says a new study shows Pasifika children in Aotearoa are 115 times more likely to be hospitalised with acute rheumatic fever than European children. The fourth State of Child Health Report showed Pasifika, Māori and children in low socio-economic areas were disproportionately affected by respiratory conditions, rheumatic fever and heart disease, skin infections, dental disease and mental health problems. Cure Kids head Frances Soutter said urgent national action was needed to ensure all tamariki and rangatahi had access to proper healthcare, housing and nutrition to reverse the trend. "Too many of our children are experiencing preventable illnesses, with the burden falling disproportionately on Māori, Pasifika, and those living in areas of high deprivation. By targeting these risk factors, we can reverse these trends and generate long-term benefits for New Zealand's population that far exceed the initial costs," Soutter said. The report - developed in collaboration with the NZ Child and Youth Epidemiology Service at the University of Otago - showed a 44 percent increase in the number of children under a year old being hospitalised with respiratory problems

over the last 20 years. It said respiratory conditions were the leading
cause of acute hospitalisations for children, with infants under one year being particularly vulnerable. The University of Auckland's Dr Anneka Anderson said the study was a "huge wake-up call" that more needed to be done to address poverty and poor living conditions and break down barriers to healthcare. She said a one-size-fits-all approach to health would only make matters worse. "Saying that we should treat everyone the same actually promotes inequity. It's a bit like saying we shouldn't have special carparks for non able-bodied people. "We have different services to try and level up the playing field, and taking that away always leads to a disaster." She said the Covid-19 pandemic had provided an ideal case study to show the power of tailoring a health response towards ethnic and cultural groups. "The government responded with a one-size-fits-all approach and we saw huge differences in vaccine uptake for Māori than for non-Māori. As soon as the control and resources were handed back to Māori providers - to provide a 'for Māori, by Māori' service - we saw the uptake increase. "So we see that this rhetoric that ethnicity doesn't count and shouldn't be taken into account for different health services hasn't worked in the past, and there's no way it's going to work in the future." Anderson said - in addition to working to address poverty and basic living wages - health services needed to be designed with a "rights based lens" to cut the inequities across the population. "We live in such a resource rich country. [Typically] in low economic countries we see these high rates of rheumatic heart disease. In Aotearoa we shouldn't be seeing those. This is a completely preventable disease. So it shouldn't be there and I think the fact that it is there is a huge wake-up call that we're not doing things

Primary health initiatives include Plunket (founded 1907), School Medical Service (established 1912), and modern integrated youth health centers. Major pediatric facilities include Starship Hospital (opened 1991) and Kidz First Children's Hospital (established 2000). 16.fileDescription: Rural New Zealand faces a critical healthcare crisis with patients dying from preventable causes due to inadequate medical services and severe resource constraints. Despite rural communities producing 80% of New Zealand's export earnings, they experience significantly higher mortality rates, limited access to healthcare facilities, and acute doctor shortages. Surgeon Vanessa Blair highlights systemic failures within the healthcare system, including cases of misdiagnosis and preventable deaths at rural hospitals lacking adequate staffing levels. Research demonstrates that rural residents experience twice the preventable disease mortality compared to urban counterparts, elevated suicide rates, and poor access to specialist services. Rural hospitals such as Taupō operate at approximately half their required staffing levels, exacerbating the healthcare equity gap. While the government has introduced workforce initiatives including accommodation allowances, locum funding, and relocation programs to attract healthcare professionals to rural areas, healthcare experts argue these measures are insufficient without substantial increases in central government funding and systemic healthcare reforms.

Non-Māori men aged 30 to 44 were 1.8 times more likely to die from preventable causes compared with their peers living in urban areas. Preventable causes included suicide - "there's scant access to specialist mental health support in the regions" - as well as workplace accidents and road crashes. Both primary care and hospital services in the regions needed a big injection of cash from central government, Bolden said. "They're not going to have a rural health service without putting more money into it. And a 4 percent rise in capitation funding [to GPs] is not going to address any of the issues." The sector was also anxiously awaiting the release of the Health Workforce Plan to deal with regional inequities, she said. Improving rural health a government "priority" Minister of Health Shane Reti said improving rural health was "an integral part of improving all health in New Zealand". The government inherited "long-standing" problems with the health workforce, but was tackling them head-on through an additional 25 medical school places and working with Waikato University on its proposal for a third medical school, he said. ByRayssa Almeida - Reporter
2024-11-29 06:28:35+13:00

Mental health patients
in New Zealand face significantly worse
experiences in primary healthcare compared to those without mental
health conditions, according to a national study conducted by the University of Otago. The study, published in the New Zealand Medical Journal, analysed responses from a Health Quality and Safety Commission survey that asked about people's experiences with general practice services. The findings revealed critical barriers to accessing care, with 26.8 percent of mental health patients unable to secure a GP appointment in the past year, compared to 19.6 percent of the general population. Deep-rooted systemic issues Ruth Cunningham Lead researcher Ruth Cunningham said the disparities reflected deep-rooted systemic issues, including stigma and the pressures on the healthcare system itself. "When the system is under stress... our cognitive biases come through, and we're even more likely to treat people differently because of those biases," she said. "In those cases... providers [need to] think about the experience that people with mental health conditions are having [at the doctor.. but [it] can become harder when the system is under stress." Cunningham emphasised the importance of medical professionals being aware of their biases and how these affect patient care. "The way in which a diagnosis of mental health conditions, problematic substance or addiction, can get in the way of providing high-quality care is not something that is often talked about, but is a very important issue." Stigma also discourages patients from seeking care, Cunningham noted. "Experiences of stigma and discrimination... understandably [lead people to] disconnect from the provider or they simply don't go back." Connection and representation The study highlighted that disparities were even more significant for Māori with mental health conditions, who consistently reported greater challenges in accessing care, feeling respected, and having their concerns heard by healthcare providers. For instance, Māori with mental health conditions were 7.7 percent more likely than non-Māori to report difficulties in
securing a GP appointment within the past year. Cunningham pointed to

the need for a more diverse healthcare workforce to improve patient-provider relationships. "For Māori, the difference in care was exacerbated... even more adverse experiences of care," she said. "This is all about connection and relationships... and increasing Māori and Pasifika healthcare workforce representation. The patient needs to connect to their providers and, if that doesn't happen, they might not come back to seek treatment." Despite the disparities, Cunningham said there were positive developments within the healthcare system. "But we must continue to listen, address biases, and ensure care meets everyone's needs. Even in a stressed system, treating people with kindness and respect remains essential." Related

18.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines health inequalities and social determinants of health in New Zealand, focusing on disparities among ethnic groups. It explores how socio-economic status, ethnicity, employment, housing, education, and environmental conditions shape health outcomes. Significant health disparities exist between Māori and Pākehā populations, with Māori experiencing lower life expectancy (73-77 years vs 80-84 years in 2012-14), and an 8-year gap between least and most deprived areas for males. Major health challenges include cancer (30% of deaths in 2015), cardiovascular diseases, tobacco use, poor nutrition, and obesity. Tobacco remains the leading preventable cause of death, with Māori adults 2.5 times more likely to smoke. Healthcare access is limited by cost, with 25-33% deferring doctor visits due to expense. The document traces New Zealand's health services evolution from fee-based systems (pre-1940s) to subsidized services (post-1938) and the 21st-century primary health organization model. It discusses culturally responsive healthcare approaches for Māori and Pacific populations, including decorated clinics and traditional healer referrals. While Asian populations showed better health outcomes, they faced language barriers. Government policy and district health boards made reducing inequalities a statutory obligation, though targeted public health initiatives have not reached all eligible populations.

This comprehensive document provides an overview of public health in New Zealand, covering disease prevention, health promotion, and population-level health inequalities from the 19th century to present. It traces the evolution of public health infrastructure, including the Department of Public Health (established 1900) and its transformation into the Ministry of Health, with major reforms in 1993 and the 2000s emphasizing district health boards.

Significant attention is given to health disparities among Māori and Pacific Island populations, who experience disproportionately high disease and premature mortality rates. The document examines evidence of health inequalities linked to socio-economic status and government responses including district health boards with statutory obligations to reduce inequalities. Additional topics include tobacco control as a public health success story, cancer screening programmes, mental health with 20% prevalence in 12 months and 47% lifetime prevalence, water safety issues (Queenstown 1984, Havelock North 2016), and the 2017 Healthy Homes Guarantee Act addressing housing standards.

The findings revealed critical barriers to accessing care, with 26.8 percent of mental health patients unable to secure a GP appointment in the past year, compared to 19.6 percent of the general population. Deep rooted systemic issues Ruth Cunningham Lead researcher Ruth Cunningham said the disparities reflected deep rooted systemic issues, including stigma and the pressures on the healthcare system itself. "When the system is under stress... our cognitive biases come through, and we're even more likely to treat people differently because of those biases," she said. "In those cases... providers [need to] think about the experience that people with mental health conditions are having [at the doctor.. but [it] can become harder when the system is under stress." Cunningham emphasised the importance of medical professionals being aware of their biases and how these affect patient care. "The way in which a diagnosis of mental health conditions, problematic substance or addiction, can get in the way of providing high quality care is not something that is often talked about, but is a very important issue." Stigma also discourages patients from seeking care, Cunningham noted. "Experiences of stigma and discrimination... understandably [lead people to] disconnect from the provider or they simply don't go back." Māori, Pacific people and young people are not being prioritised when it comes to accessing mental health support, a new report has found, despite evidence clearly demonstrating these groups need a higher level of support. The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission has reported that fewer people are able to access kaupapa Māori primary mental health services, and that funding for these services has not kept pace with other mental health investment. Only 29 percent of Māori who access specialist service use kaupapa Māori services, and young people are increasingly being declined for specialist help after being referred.
